title: I Have a Dream
author: Rashmi Bansal
bigIdea: Rashmi Bansal's third book profiles social entrepreneurs — Indians who built businesses with a mission beyond profit: education for slum kids, solar power for villages, healthcare for the poor. Her message: you don't have to choose between making money and changing the world — the best social enterprises do both, because a sustainable mission needs a sustainable business. The dreamers in this book prove that India's biggest problems are its biggest business opportunities, and that the entrepreneur's heart matters as much as the entrepreneur's spreadsheet.

lessons.title: The Dream That Pays: Mission and Margin Together
lessons.summary: Bansal's founders refuse the false choice between profit and purpose. The school that charges slum parents a little but delivers real learning, the solar company that sells to villages at a margin — each proves that a mission without a business model dies, and a business without a mission hollows out. The lesson: don't choose between doing good and doing well; design the model where the good IS the business. The most durable social change is the kind that pays for itself, because it can scale without depending on donations forever.
lessons.example: Bansal profiles an education venture that charges the poor a small fee and delivers quality — profitable enough to grow, mission-driven enough to matter. The fee was the discipline; the mission was the fuel.
lessons.action: Redesign one idea as 'mission + margin': who pays, what changes, and how the two reinforce each other? Write the one-line model.

lessons.title: The Slow Road: Social Change Doesn't Move at Startup Speed
lessons.summary: These founders measure progress in years, not quarters — winning trust in a village, changing a habit, building a school that survives its founder. Bansal's lesson: the most important problems resist the 'move fast and break things' playbook; they reward patience and trust. The lesson isn't 'go slow' but 'match your pace to the problem': quick wins for product problems, patient compounding for people problems. The founder who treats a community like a market to be hacked will be rejected; the one who treats it like a family to be served earns loyalty no competitor can buy.
lessons.example: A founder Bansal profiles spent years earning a village's trust before her health program took root — the slow phase looked like failure and was actually the entire strategy.
lessons.action: Identify one 'people problem' in your work that needs patience, not speed. Redefine success for it as trust built, not tasks done.

lessons.title: The Founder's Fire: Mission Sustains What Money Can't
lessons.summary: When these ventures faced crises — funding gaps, burnout, betrayal — what kept them going was not the business plan but the fire: a personal connection to the problem. Bansal shows that mission-driven founders persist through failures that purely commercial founders abandon, because the failure isn't just theirs — it's the community's too. The lesson: choose problems you personally care about, because the care is the capital that survives the dark years. The founder whose motivation is deep survives the shallow times; the one whose motivation is shallow quits at the first valley.
lessons.example: One founder, facing collapse, sold his own house to keep the school running — an act no investor spreadsheet explains, only the fire does. The mission was the balance sheet that mattered.
lessons.action: Write the problem you care about most and why it's personal. Re-read it the next time motivation dips — the fire is the fuel.

lessons.title: Funding Is a Means: Don't Let the Money Own the Mission
lessons.summary: Bansal's founders navigate the grant-versus-business tension: grants can distort (you serve the donor's metrics) and investors can distort (you chase the exit). Her lesson: funding is fuel, not direction — the founder who lets the money set the mission ends up with someone else's dream. The discipline: know your non-negotiables before you raise money, and choose funders who buy your vision rather than renting it. The same applies to any venture: the capital that comes with strings pulls the steering wheel; keep your hand on it.
lessons.example: A founder refused a large grant that required abandoning her core program — the grant would have doubled her budget and halved her mission. The refusal looked foolish; the mission survived.
lessons.action: List your non-negotiables before any funding or big partnership. Refuse any money that would break them — write the refusal criteria now.

lessons.title: The Ripple: One Person's Dream Becomes Many Lives
lessons.summary: Bansal's closing portraits show impact as a ripple: the student who becomes a teacher, the villager who becomes a trainer, the community that stops needing the NGO. The lesson: the deepest success metric is not output but independence — have you made yourself unnecessary? The leader, teacher or founder whose work empowers others to stand alone has created the only growth that lasts. The ripple is the proof: when the dream becomes many people's, it was never just yours.
lessons.example: The school that trained its own teachers, the solar company whose technicians were villagers — each built the exit of its own dependency. The founder's greatest achievement was becoming optional.
lessons.action: Define success as independence: what would it look like if your team, students or community stopped needing you? Build one 'exit of dependency' this quarter.

lessons.title: The Dream Is the Business Plan: Start With Why You Care
lessons.summary: Every founder in the book started the same way: with a problem they couldn't ignore, not a market they researched. Bansal's final lesson: the best business plans begin as personal outrage or love, and the plan comes after. The lesson: stop waiting for the perfect pitch; start with the thing you can't stop thinking about. The market research matters later; the care matters first. The dream is not the enemy of the business plan — it is the seed the plan grows from. If you don't dream it first, you'll never plan it properly.
lessons.example: Bansal's founders routinely began with one angry question — 'why do these kids not have schools?' — and the organizations grew from the question, not from a consulting report.
lessons.action: Write the one problem that keeps you awake. That's your seed — sketch the smallest possible version of the answer this week.

quotes: The most durable social change is the kind that pays for itself.
The care is the capital that survives the dark years.
Your greatest achievement is making yourself unnecessary.
actionPlan: Write your 'mission + margin' model in one line.
Match your pace to the problem — patience for people problems.
Identify your personal fire and keep it visible.
List your non-negotiables before taking any money.
Start with the problem you can't ignore — sketch the smallest answer.
tagline: Social entrepreneurs who made mission pay.
oneLiner: Rashmi Bansal profiles Indians who built businesses that change lives — proving mission and margin can coexist when the good IS the business.
caveat: The dream-building genre — vision, purpose, scale — has a shadow the books never mention: WeWork India's parent rode the dream of 'elevating the world's consciousness' to a $47 billion valuation and then the dream met accounting, and the valuation became a lesson in what dreams without economics are worth. The caveat for every dreamer: Martin Luther King's dream worked because it was attached to a real movement with real costs and real people. The startup dream works the same way — the vision is fuel, but the business must still be true. Have a dream; also have a P&L. The world pays for outcomes, not for consciousness-raising.
